title: Asteroid Collision
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly rescanning and resolving collisions versus a single stack-based pass with cascading resolution.

blocks.text: We are given an array asteroids of integers representing asteroids in a row. For each asteroid, the ABSOLUTE VALUE represents its size, and the SIGN represents its direction (positive means moving right, negative means moving left). Each asteroid moves at the same speed. Find out the state of the asteroids after all collisions: two asteroids moving in the same direction never meet; when two meet, the smaller one explodes (if both are the same size, both explode).

blocks.caption: A stack of surviving right-moving asteroids naturally models collisions: a new left-mover only ever collides with whatever is currently on top

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of non-zero integers, each representing an asteroid's size (absolute value) and direction (sign)"],["Output","The array of surviving asteroids after all collisions have resolved"],["Goal","Correctly simulate every collision (including chains of multiple collisions) in a single linear pass"],["Constraints","2 <= asteroids.length <= 10^4; -1000 <= asteroids[i] <= 1000; asteroids[i] != 0"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A NEW element can only collide with the MOST RECENTLY surviving element (moving toward it)","A stack naturally represents \"the most recently surviving right-mover,\" which is exactly what a new left-mover needs to check against"],["A single collision can trigger a CHAIN of further collisions (destroying multiple stack entries)","A while loop (not a single if) that keeps resolving collisions against the stack's top as long as the current asteroid survives"]]}

blocks.text: Only a RIGHT-moving asteroid followed (later in the array) by a LEFT-moving asteroid can ever collide, since same-direction asteroids never catch up to each other, and a left-mover followed by a right-mover are moving AWAY from each other. Whenever a collision happens, the smaller asteroid is destroyed (or both, if equal size), and this can cascade if the surviving asteroid then collides with yet another one behind it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Bumper Cars Only Ever Colliding Head-On
blocks.text: Imagine bumper cars in a single row, where cars moving RIGHT can only ever be hit from behind by a car moving LEFT that catches up to them (or rather, moves toward them from the right side). Whenever a car heading left encounters a car (or several, in sequence) still heading right, they collide, and the smaller car is knocked out, exactly like an elimination bracket, potentially eliminating several right-moving cars in a row if the left-moving car is big enough to survive each collision.

blocks.caption: A new left-moving asteroid repeatedly collides with the stack's top (a surviving right-mover) until either it explodes, ties, or survives past everything smaller

blocks.text: Before simulating collisions by repeatedly scanning the array for adjacent colliding pairs (awkward and inefficient), notice that a stack of surviving right-movers naturally represents exactly "what a new left-mover could collide with," resolving even chains of collisions in a single forward pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Only a right-moving asteroid can ever be "caught up to" by a later left-moving one; same-direction pairs and left-then-right pairs never collide at all.

Observation 2: Walking through the asteroids left to right, maintaining a stack of surviving right-movers: a new RIGHT-mover simply gets pushed (nothing to collide with yet).

Observation 3: A new LEFT-mover must be checked against the stack's CURRENT TOP (the most recently surviving right-mover): if the top is smaller, it explodes and the check REPEATS against whatever is now exposed as the new top (a potential CHAIN of collisions); if equal, both explode; if the top is bigger, the new left-mover explodes and nothing further happens.

Observation 4: This repeating collision check (a while loop, not a single comparison) is exactly what correctly resolves chains of multiple collisions triggered by one incoming left-mover.

This is a direct stack-based simulation: a stack of surviving right-movers, with each new left-mover repeatedly resolving collisions against the stack's top until either it explodes, ties, or survives.

Repeatedly scan the array for the first adjacent pair where a right-mover is immediately followed by a left-mover, resolve that single collision, and restart scanning (since a resolved collision can create a new adjacent colliding pair).

items: Scan for the first position where a positive value is immediately followed by a negative value.
Resolve that collision (removing the smaller, or both if equal), then step back one position (since the newly adjacent pair might ALSO collide) and continue scanning from there.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Restarting the check one position back after each resolved collision correctly handles chains, since a newly exposed pair might also collide.
This directly mirrors the collision rules, but requires potentially many rescans and expensive list modifications (removals from the middle of the array).

blocks.text: Correctly resolves every collision, including cascading chains, since it always re-checks the newly adjacent pair after each resolution.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, due to repeated array modifications and rescanning.
Space: O(n), for the working array.
Limitation: repeatedly modifying and rescanning the array is inefficient; a stack-based single forward pass resolves the identical collision logic in O(n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force repeatedly rescans and modifies the array. Instead, maintain a stack of surviving right-moving asteroids. Walk through the array once: a right-mover is simply pushed; a left-mover repeatedly collides with the stack's top (in a while loop) as long as it keeps winning, correctly resolving chains of collisions without ever needing to rescan.

Walk through asteroids with a stack. For each value a: while a is negative, the stack is non-empty, and its top is positive, resolve one collision (pop if the top is smaller, pop and stop if equal, or just stop if the top is bigger, in which case a is destroyed). If a survives this process, push it.
Use a stack of surviving right-moving asteroids, resolving each new left-mover's collisions in a while loop to correctly handle chains.

blocks.text: The surviving stack is [10], matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once across the entire simulation.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

The stack always represents exactly the CURRENT set of surviving asteroids, in left-to-right order; since only a right-mover can ever be threatened by a LATER left-mover, and the most recently added right-mover is always the FIRST one any new left-mover would reach, checking against the stack's top (repeatedly, as it changes) correctly and completely resolves every collision, including chains, without ever needing to look further back than necessary.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A right-mover (positive value)","Always simply pushed; nothing behind it can threaten it yet"],["A left-mover meets a smaller right-mover on top","That right-mover explodes (popped); the left-mover continues checking against the new top"],["A left-mover meets an equal-size right-mover","Both explode; the left-mover does not survive to check further"],["A left-mover meets a bigger right-mover","The left-mover explodes; the right-mover survives unchanged"]]}

items: The while loop's three conditions (still alive, negative direction, a positive top exists) together correctly identify exactly when a collision check should occur.
The three-way comparison (top smaller, equal, or bigger) directly maps onto the three possible collision outcomes described in the problem.
Only pushing when "alive" remains true at the end correctly excludes any left-mover that was destroyed during its collision chain.

blocks.text: When new elements can only "attack" the most recently surviving element (and that attack can cascade further back if it keeps winning), a stack combined with a while loop (not a single comparison) correctly and efficiently resolves the entire simulation, including chains, in a single forward pass.

items: Using a single if instead of a while loop for the collision check, which would fail to correctly resolve chains of multiple collisions.
Forgetting that a right-mover following a LEFT-mover (in that order) can never collide, since they move apart from each other.
Mishandling the "equal size" case, forgetting that BOTH asteroids explode (not just one).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["All asteroids moving in the same direction","No collisions ever occur; every asteroid survives"],["A single very large left-mover meeting many small right-movers in sequence","It survives, destroying all of them in a chain, since it is bigger than each one it meets"],["Two equal-size asteroids moving toward each other","Both explode, leaving neither behind"]]}

items: Explicitly stating "only a right-mover immediately followed (later) by a left-mover can ever collide" up front clarifies the core rule before diving into the stack-based simulation details.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Simulate collisions where a new element can chain-eliminate multiple previous survivors" points toward a stack combined with a while loop (not a single check) for the collision resolution.

items: How would you count the TOTAL number of collisions that occurred, not just the final surviving state? Add a counter, incrementing it once for each pop (and once more for a tie, since both asteroids are destroyed).
What is the maximum possible stack size during the simulation? Up to n, if every asteroid moves in the same direction (right), since no collisions ever occur.

How would this change if asteroids could have EQUAL speeds but different STARTING positions, not just uniform speed? The core collision-order logic would remain similar, though determining WHICH pairs actually meet would require additional timing calculations beyond simple left-to-right order.

A direct application of the "stack resolves cascading interactions with the most recent survivor" pattern, conceptually similar to Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String elsewhere in this category, both using a while loop against the stack's top to correctly handle chains.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (stack of surviving right-movers): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-based collision simulation with cascading resolution

Core Idea: A stack of surviving right-movers lets each new left-mover repeatedly collide with the current top (in a while loop) until it explodes, ties, or survives, correctly handling chains of collisions
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Only a right-mover followed later by a left-mover can ever collide; a while loop (not a single if) is essential for correctly resolving collision chains
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Push right-movers; a left-mover repeatedly fights the stack's top (smaller pops, equal both pop, bigger survives)
